1. The frames show a grid of many small houses. Each house stands for one historical scenario, and the grid compares buying with renting over ten years. A lit house means the buyer came out ahead after ten years. A dark house means the renter came out ahead. The header says the data come from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. It is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. At first (frames 1–2) every house is dark. The houses then light up (frames 3–6), starting from the front-left corner and spreading toward the back and right. By frame 6, most of the grid is lit. A band of dark houses remains along the back and right edge.

3. In most of the historical cases shown, buying beat renting over a ten-year hold. Renting came out ahead in a minority of cases. Buying is not a guaranteed win, and the result depends on when you buy and on the prices and rates at that time. The label says this is history and not a forecast, so it doesn't predict what will happen to you.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has often paid off over a ten-year horizon. They might also take away that it sometimes doesn't, so the timing and the length of time you stay in the home matter.

5. The advice in 4 is my own inference. The picture and text only show the lit and dark proportions and the "history, not a forecast" caveat. They never tell the viewer to buy or to rent.
